summary: Describes a possible mechanism for controlling the rate of acknowledgment traffic in TCP, using cooperation between the data sender and receiver. It is aimed at links where the return path is constrained. It is informational and does not define a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Every TCP receiver sends acknowledgements back to the sender. This memo describes a way for the sender to ask the receiver to send fewer of them when the return path is full, and for the two ends to work out when that is needed from the acknowledgements alone.

subtitle: Making a TCP receiver send fewer acknowledgements when the return path is congested.

tldr.problem: On a link where the path back is narrower than the path out, the acknowledgements travelling back can fill the return path and add delay to the data that is flowing forward.
tldr.mechanism: The sender watches the acknowledgements it receives for gaps that show an acknowledgement was lost or marked, and tells the receiver to acknowledge less often by sending a new ratio value in a TCP option. A lost acknowledgement doubles the ratio; a quiet period lowers it again.
tldr.outcome: The document specifies the mechanism in detail, lists the cases where it can misfire, and leaves the recommendation on whether to use it in TCP open until it has been evaluated more fully.

facts.value: 2, one ACK for every two data packets

Minimum ACK rate

today: RFC 5690 is an Informational memo published in February 2010, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It specifies the mechanism and discusses the complications, but states that it defers a recommendation on using the mechanism in TCP until it has been evaluated more fully. The two TCP option numbers were never allocated by IANA as part of this document.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The document describes a congestion control mechanism for TCP acknowledgements. It is based on the acknowledgement congestion control in the CCID 2 profile of DCCP, which is itself a successor to a mechanism proposed by Balakrishnan and others.

Throughout the document the sender is the host sending data and the receiver the host sending acknowledgements in response. In the DCCP mechanism the receiver uses an ACK Ratio R reported to it by the sender, sending roughly one acknowledgement packet for every R data packets received. The DCCP sender keeps the acknowledgement rate roughly TCP-friendly by watching the acknowledgement stream for lost and marked acknowledgement packets and changing the ratio accordingly: for every round-trip time containing such an event, that is, a lost or marked acknowledgement, it halves the acknowledgement rate by doubling the ratio; for every round-trip time with no such event, it additively increases the acknowledgement rate by lowering the ratio gradually.

The goal here is to explore a similar mechanism for TCP. The assumption is that in some environments with congestion on the reverse path, reducing the sending rate of acknowledgement traffic that traverses the congested path can help reduce the congestion itself. Where the reverse path is congested but TCP acknowledgement traffic does not appreciably contribute to that congestion, the goal is for the mechanism to have a minimal negative effect on the performance of the connection.

Adding such control as an option in TCP would need four things: agreement between the hosts on using it, through a new TCP option called the ACK Congestion Control Permitted option; a way for the sender to detect lost and ECN-marked pure acknowledgement packets; a way to adjust the ACK Ratio; and a way to tell the receiver a new value for the ratio, through a second new TCP option called the ACK Ratio option.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is to let the sender slow down the acknowledgements, but only when the acknowledgements themselves are being lost or marked as congested. The two ends agree on this during connection setup and then exchange the ratio in ordinary data packets.

sections.title: Overview of the Mechanism
sections.content:
The example in the document has TCP host B as the connection initiator. During connection initiation, host B sends an ACK Congestion Control Permitted option on its SYN or SYN/ACK packet, which allows host A, now the sender, to send instructions to host B, now the receiver, about the ACK Ratio to use when answering data packets. Host A sends the same option, so with the negotiation of ECN-Capability the receiver can also send its acknowledgement packets as ECN-capable.

The receiver starts with an ACK Ratio of two, generally sending one acknowledgement packet for every two data packets received. If the sender then detects a lost or ECN-marked acknowledgement packet, it sends an ACK Ratio option of four, and the receiver changes to a ratio of four, sending one acknowledgement for at most four data packets. The sender uses appropriate byte counting and rate-based pacing when responding to those acknowledgements. When the sender detects a period with no lost acknowledgement packets, it sends an ACK Ratio option of three, and the receiver goes back to sending one acknowledgement for at most three data packets.

The goal is to control the pure acknowledgement traffic on the path from the receiver back to the sender. The approach is end-to-end, as the DCCP approach is, but it can also take advantage of explicit congestion information from the network, conveyed by ECN, when it is available. The ECN specification prohibits a TCP receiver from setting the ECT code points in IP packets carrying pure acknowledgements, but only as long as the receiver does not implement any form of acknowledgement congestion control.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver starts by acknowledging every second data packet. If the sender notices an acknowledgement went missing, it asks the receiver to acknowledge every fourth packet instead. Once acknowledgements stop going missing, it asks for every third packet again.

sections.title: The Two TCP Options
sections.content:
The two ends negotiate the use of acknowledgement congestion control with the ACK Congestion Control Permitted option, whose number would be allocated by IANA. The option can only be sent on packets with the SYN bit set. If end point A receives the option from end point B, the two may use acknowledgement congestion control on the pure acknowledgements sent from B to A, which means A may send ACK Ratio values for B to use. Equally, if A does not receive the option from B, A knows not to waste its time detecting lost acknowledgement packets and sending ratio values.

If B receives the option from A and also sent the option to A, and ECN-Capability has been negotiated, then B can send its pure acknowledgement packets as ECN-capable. The option itself is two octets long: a kind byte and a length byte.

The sender uses the ACK Ratio option to pass the ratio value to the receiver. It is three octets long: a kind byte, a length byte and the ratio itself. The option is only sent on data packets, and because TCP delivers data reliably, the sender can tell whether the receiver has received an ACK Ratio option.

With a ratio of R, the receiver should send one pure acknowledgement for every R newly received data packets, unless the delayed acknowledgement timer expires first. A receiver could keep a counter that rises by one for each new data packet and send an acknowledgement when it reaches R, resetting the counter whenever a pure or piggybacked acknowledgement is sent. If the receiver has buffer limitations it may have to acknowledge K packets for some K less than the current ratio, and the sender could observe from the acknowledgements that the receiver is acknowledging less than R packets. Because lost or marked acknowledgements can happen before any data packets have been lost, the sender could raise the ratio even during the initial slow start.
sections.plainLanguage: Two small options carry the whole mechanism. One is sent only during connection setup and says whether the sender may ask the receiver to slow down. The other rides on ordinary data packets and carries the current ratio.

sections.title: Detecting Lost Acknowledgements and Changing the Ratio
sections.content:
The sender uses its knowledge of the ratio to infer when an acknowledgement has been lost. In the absence of dropped or reordered acknowledgements, each new acknowledgement acknowledges at most R additional data packets, so if the sender receives an acknowledgement acknowledging more than R data packets and no later acknowledgement acknowledging a strict subset of them, it can infer that an acknowledgement packet was dropped. The use of SACK options helps here. In the other direction, in the absence of dropped data packets and of delayed acknowledgements caused by the receiver's timer, each new pure acknowledgement acknowledges at least R additional data packets, and the sender needs to take no action when it receives an acknowledgement acknowledging fewer than R.

Out-of-order data packets complicate this. With a ratio of at most two the receiver sends a duplicate acknowledgement for every out-of-order data packet, and the sender should be able to detect lost duplicate acknowledgements by counting the ones that arrive between the start of the loss event and the first full or partial acknowledgement, and comparing that with the number that should have arrived. With a ratio above two the receiver does not send a duplicate acknowledgement for every out-of-order packet, and for simplicity the sender does not attempt to detect lost acknowledgements during loss events in the forward direction: as soon as it infers a loss of a forward-path data packet it stops looking for reverse-path acknowledgement loss, and restarts once a new cumulative acknowledgement covering the retransmitted data arrives. The sender also should not try to detect lost acknowledgements during a loss recovery period, because retransmitted data filling holes in the receiver's sequence space makes the cumulative acknowledgement jump irregularly.

Three constraints always hold. The ratio is an integer. It does not exceed max(2, cwnd/(K times MSS)) rounded up, for K equal to 2, so the receiver generally sends at least two acknowledgements in response to a window of at least four full-sized segments. And if the congestion window is at least four full-sized segments, the ratio is at least two, which means a ratio of one is allowed only when the congestion window is at most three full-sized segments.

Within those constraints, for each congestion window of data with lost or marked acknowledgement packets the ratio is doubled, and for each cwnd/(MSS times (R squared minus R)) consecutive congestion windows with no lost or marked acknowledgement packets the ratio is decreased by one. For a constant congestion window these changes give an acknowledgement sending rate that is roughly TCP-friendly. The sender need not keep the ratio completely up to date and may rate-limit renegotiation to once every four or five round-trip times, or once every second or two, but should not change it more than once per round-trip time, and should check that the receiver has acknowledged a data packet carrying the previous ratio before sending a new one. If congestion on the reverse path is heavy enough, all the acknowledgements are dropped and the sender falls back on an exponentially backed-off timeout, which reduces the sending rate on the forward path and so on the reverse path as well.

The receiver's behaviour for out-of-order data is also specified. With a ratio of at most two the receiver still sends an immediate duplicate acknowledgement when an out-of-order segment arrives. With a ratio above two the receiver still sends an immediate duplicate acknowledgement for each of the first three out-of-order segments in a reordering event, and after that it returns to sending an acknowledgement for every R segments. In no case may a receiver withhold an acknowledgement for more than 500 ms.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender can tell that an acknowledgement was lost because the next acknowledgement covers more data than the ratio allows. When that happens it doubles the ratio, and when acknowledgements stop going missing it lowers the ratio again, one step at a time.

sections.title: Possible Complications
sections.content:
The document works through a list of cases where the mechanism may not behave as intended.

A receiver may send a delayed acknowledgement for a single packet even when the ratio is two or more. This should not cause false positives, because the sender only infers a loss when no data packet has been lost and an acknowledgement arrives acknowledging more than R new packets. It can cause false negatives, where the sender cannot detect the loss of an acknowledgement sent as a delayed acknowledgement. That seems acceptable, and would result in approximate rather than exact control, which is better than none.

With two-way traffic the sender may not always be able to infer that a pure acknowledgement was lost, because the receiver could send a pure acknowledgement for packet K and soon afterwards a data packet for the reverse flow with the same acknowledgement number, so the loss of the pure acknowledgement is invisible. The problem is limited: the sender fails to detect only an acknowledgement followed by a data packet with the same acknowledgement number. If the reverse path is dominated by data traffic, the data congestion control matters more; if it is dominated by pure acknowledgements, the sender will detect the loss of most of them.

Acknowledgement packets can also be reordered on the reverse path. The sender could use a parallel mechanism to the duplicate-acknowledgement threshold, or more robustly wait a whole round-trip time before inferring that an acknowledgement was lost.

Other cases listed include an abrupt change in the path the acknowledgements take, corruption, acknowledgements that do not contribute to congestion, TCP implementations that skip acknowledgement packets, and router or middlebox mechanisms that generate acknowledgements. Data-limited senders are also discussed, since a sender with little data to send does not generate many acknowledgements to be lost.

The document also notes that evaluating the mechanism needs two parts: its effect on an individual TCP connection, and its effect on aggregate traffic, including whether it increases the burstiness of aggregate traffic or otherwise changes traffic dynamics. One possible benefit is reduced contention in wireless links, shared Ethernet and other environments where forward and reverse traffic interfere, although contention on the shared medium does not necessarily result in dropped acknowledgement packets and so would not necessarily be detected. Keep-alive packets and window probes are not affected by the mechanism, and the receiver uses a delayed acknowledgement timer alongside the ratio, so acknowledgement congestion control never causes a receiver to delay indefinitely.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender can only guess that an acknowledgement was lost, and several things can make that guess wrong: a delayed acknowledgement, traffic flowing in both directions at once, and acknowledgements arriving out of order. The document says these cases make the control approximate rather than exact.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document asks what incentives the sender and the receiver have to cheat, and what avenues for cheating exist. As long as acknowledgement congestion control is optional, neither host can be forced to use it, so it will only be used if one of them expects to gain something. As long as it stays optional for TCP, there is little incentive to cheat on the version that does not use ECN, because nothing requires TCP hosts to respond to dropped acknowledgements.

ECN-capable acknowledgements open more avenues. If the ends can have acknowledgement packets marked rather than dropped, and can then avoid the acknowledgement congestion control that goes with ECN on those packets, they would have an incentive to cheat. A sender could cheat by not telling the receiver to use a higher ratio, and the receiver would have a hard time detecting that. A receiver could cheat by ignoring the ratio it was given, but the sender could detect that easily. A receiver could also cheat by not using acknowledgement congestion control and still sending acknowledgements as ECN-capable, so acknowledgement congestion control is not a necessary part of that particular cheating.

Routers and middleboxes would have a hard time detecting a receiver that cheats by sending acknowledgements as ECN-capable when it should not. A router can only know whether the receiver was authorised to do so if it can see traffic on both the forward and reverse paths and has watched the SYN and SYN/ACK packets, including the TCP options. If acknowledgement congestion control was negotiated, the router can only tell whether the receiver is using it correctly if it can watch the ACK Ratio options sent from the sender. Even then it cannot always tell whether the sender is behaving correctly, because acknowledgements may be dropped after they have left the router; but if the router does see the ACK Ratio options it can tell whether the sender is accounting correctly for the acknowledgements dropped or marked on the path from the receiver to the router.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the mechanism is optional, there is little reason for either end to cheat on it. With ECN in the picture there is more room, and a router in the middle would have to watch both directions to detect a receiver that fakes it.
